141.quote_or_event: “You have abandoned your own wife, but now you sneak glances at other women. God is not found by wearing religious robes; you are utterly miserable!”
141.explanation: Guru Arjan exposes the man who makes a show of religion while his eye strays to other men's wives, and says such a life brings only misery.
141.tie_back: The Kural says those who have truly grasped virtue never fall into this folly; Guru Arjan shows that outward religiosity without that understanding does not prevent it.
141.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1348, Raag Prabhati, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
141._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: both link coveting another's wife to a failure of real understanding, though the hymn targets religious hypocrisy rather than calling the desire folly in so many words.

142.quote_or_event: “You gaze upon the wives of others, O my soul; you steal and commit evil deeds.”
142.explanation: Guru Nanak rebukes the wayward soul for eyeing other men's wives and joining that to theft and other wrongs.
142.tie_back: The Kural ranks the man who lingers at a neighbour's door for his wife as the greatest fool among wrongdoers; Guru Nanak names the same longing gaze among the soul's chief failings.
142.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
142._accuracy_note: Partial: shared condemnation of desiring another's wife, but no ranking of wrongdoers and no image of waiting at another's gate.

143.quote_or_event: In the Charitropakhyan of the Dasam Granth, the narrator recalls being taught never, even by mistake or in a dream, to go to another's wife's bed, and warns that such love is like a sharp dagger and an invitation to death.
143.explanation: The passage presents adultery as something that kills the one who commits it, not only the one wronged.
143.tie_back: The Kural says those who plot against the home of a trusting friend are no different from the dead; this text likewise treats such desire as death already working in the body.
143.source: Dasam Granth, Charitropakhyan (Charitar 21), verses 51-53 as numbered on BaniDB (attributed to Guru Gobind Singh; authorship contested)
143._accuracy_note: Next-best: used because no SGGS line on betraying a trusting friend's household was found; the Charitropakhyan's authorship is contested within Sikhism, and the passage lacks the Kural's stress on betrayed trust.

144.quote_or_event: “Ahalyaa was the wife of Gautam the seer. Seeing her, Indra was enticed. When he received a thousand marks of disgrace on his body, then he felt regret in his mind.”
144.explanation: Guru Nanak retells how Indra, king of the gods, lusted after a sage's wife and was marked with disgrace, regretting it only afterwards.
144.tie_back: The Kural asks what greatness is worth if a man enters another's home without a moment's thought; Indra's story shows the highest rank undone by exactly that thoughtlessness.
144.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1344, Raag Prabhati, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
144._accuracy_note: Strong fit: greatness ruined by unreflecting desire for another's wife, with regret coming too late; the same verse is also used for Kural 25, and Guru Nanak cites the myth as illustration, not as belief in Indra.

145.quote_or_event: “Those men who go out to enjoy other men's women shall suffer in shame.”
145.explanation: Guru Arjan says plainly that men who pursue other men's wives will be put to shame.
145.tie_back: The Kural warns that the man who thinks it easy to cross into another's home earns a disgrace that never dies; Guru Arjan names the same shame as the certain outcome.
145.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1362, Phunhay Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
145._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the shame that follows adultery; the Kural's contrast between a moment's ease and undying blame is not spelled out.

146.quote_or_event: “Caught in slander and attachment to the wealth and women of others, they eat poison and suffer in pain.”
146.explanation: Guru Nanak describes those drawn to others' wealth, others' women and slander as eating poison and living in pain.
146.tie_back: The Kural lists enmity, sin, fear and disgrace as companions that never leave the adulterer; Guru Nanak likewise says this desire brings lasting suffering.
146.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1255, Raag Malar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
146._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the suffering that follows, but there is no fourfold list, and adultery is grouped with greed and slander rather than treated alone.

147.quote_or_event: “The Sikh ought to treat beautiful women of others as his mothers, sisters, and daughters.”
147.explanation: In a pauri on what a Sikh ought to do, Bhai Gurdas makes regarding other men's women as mother, sister or daughter a mark of the true disciple.
147.tie_back: The Kural defines the true householder by his not desiring another's wife; Bhai Gurdas defines the true Sikh, himself a householder, by the same restraint.
147.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 11 (English translation as published on BaniDB and searchgurbani.com)
147._accuracy_note: Strong fit: both define the virtuous person by this one restraint; Bhai Gurdas is early and authoritative exegesis, not scripture.

148.quote_or_event: “whose eyes do not gaze upon the beauty of others' wives,”
148.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan lists not looking at other men's wives with desire among the marks of the rare, truly pure person.
148.tie_back: The Kural moves the line from the act to the gaze and calls this restraint the fullness of conduct; Guru Arjan likewise makes the undesiring eye a mark of holiness.
148.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 9, Pauri 1, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
148._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on restraint of the gaze; the Kural's reframing of this restraint as 'great manliness' has no exact Gurbani counterpart. The same pauri supplies Kural 149.

149.quote_or_event: “whose eyes do not gaze upon the beauty of others' wives, … - O Nanak, among millions, there is scarcely one such 'touch-nothing Saint'.”
149.explanation: Guru Arjan closes his portrait of the truly pure person, whose eyes do not covet others' wives, by saying such a one is rare among millions.
149.tie_back: The Kural asks who in the whole sea-girt world deserves every good and answers: those who do not embrace another's wife; Guru Arjan likewise singles out such a person as rare and honoured.
149.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 9, Pauri 1, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
149._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the pauri praises the restrained person as rare rather than promising him every blessing, and it lists other virtues too; it repeats the source used for Kural 148.

150.quote_or_event: “Abandoning his own wife, he is engrossed in sexual desire; his thoughts are on the wives of others.”
150.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a man who has left his wife for a renunciant's life only to find his mind fixed on other men's wives.
150.tie_back: The Kural holds that even a man who fails at much else must keep this one boundary; Guru Nanak shows a man who has given up much and still fails at this very point.
150.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1013, Raag Maru, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
150._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it condemns the same desire and reflects the Sikh critique of renunciation, but lacks the Kural's realistic concession that this is a minimum even for the imperfect.
